course_details.Overview of class: Nanotechnology involves the creation and use of small structures at the nanometer scale. This length is around a thousand times less than the diameter of a human hair, with DNA widths 1-2 nm. For 25 years, Northwestern University has been a global leader in nanoscience research spanning the basics and applications of nanomaterials in medicine, electronic and photonic devices, and photovoltaics. Our university also houses state-of-the-art instruments and tools to carry out research at the nanoscale. This seminar will cover all aspects of nanoscience and nanotechnology, with an emphasis on the groundbreaking work at Northwestern so that students can be exposed to current research. Students will have opportunities to explain an idea in nanoscience to a general audience and assess nanotechnology concerns raised in media reports.

course_details.Overview of class:
Energy, Compute, and Material Abundance and the Energy Transition

Electricity demand in the US and globally has entered into a new regime of growth, powered by rapid scaling of data centers in light of AI, combined with reshoring and electrification of manufacturing. Abundant compute has become a prerequisite for progress across science and industry, and abundant compute rests in turn on abundant energy and on abundant materials: the metals, chemicals, and manufactured components from which generation, storage, transmission, and the chips themselves are built.

This considerable demand growth will need to be fulfilled rapidly; with firm guarantees re: the dependability of the electricity; and affordably. More and more of this energy will have to be lower in its CO2 intensity than has been legacy energy production. The same applies on the materials side, where supply chains for critical minerals, and for bulk industrial materials such as steel, cement, and silicon, will need to grow quickly, securely, and at lower carbon intensity.

This will entail rapid progress in solar and wind with storage; geothermal; nuclear; and blue power. Looking more broadly across sectors, it will require innovative sustainable fuels and chemicals to power transportation, to feed the needs of industry, and to fulfill the growing energy requirements of individuals, including in high-growth emerging economies. It will also require new materials, and new routes to making and recycling familiar ones, since materials constraints bind as tightly as do energy constraints.

We will explore issues of a scientific and engineering nature; as well as of systems, economics, and policy; relating to achieving the needed growth in energy, materials, and compute across the course of the energy transition. We will study the global potential, as well as the realistic technical capacity, of the major current and future contributors to the energy mix, together with the materials and data-center buildout that these depend on; look at areas of science and technology that require advances to enable sustainable growth and maintain global competitiveness; and consider the links to national and international economics and politics.

course_details.Overview of class:
The course covers elementary physical chemistry. Topics include chemical reaction kinetics and mechanisms and thermodynamics applied to chemical processes with an emphasis on gas phase and acid-base reactions, phase and solubility equilibria, and electrochemistry. The course title, "Advanced Physical Chemistry" implies faster coverage, more depth, and challenging problems compared to a standard General Chemistry course. Typically there are three lectures each week in addition to a discussion session and a laboratory lecture.

Must be taken concurrently with the CHEM 182-0 laboratory course.

course_details.Overview of class: The design of synthetic routes to natural products and other medicinally relevant organic compounds will be covered in detail. Retrosynthetic analysis, substructure keying, and pattern recognition, along with other methods for synthetic planning will be discussed within the context of specific case studies. Classic and modern organic reactions, including asymmetric synthesis and catalysis, will be introduced and their application in synthetic planning examined. Case studies will include the synthesis of terpenes, alkaloids, polyketides, steroids, proteins and pharmaceuticals. The end result should be that students are familiar with the important issues associated with synthesis and gain intimate knowledge of a wide variety of chemical reactions. Ultimately, when presented with a given molecule, students should be able to develop a reasonable synthesis plan based on firm ideas and reliable transformations.

course_details.Overview of class:
This graduate level course explores the microscopic dynamics at atomic and molecular levels that give rise to the macroscopic chemical kinetics that are typically understood by a rate of a chemical reaction or process. The course covers a full range of chemical dynamics, beginning with elementary dynamics occurring in gas phases and going up through more complex dynamics of molecular ensembles in condensed phase environments and at interfaces. Our discussion necessarily includes modern spectroscopic methods (steady state and time-resolved spanning terahertz, infrared, visible, UV, and X-ray spectral ranges) that are used to quantify and interpret chemical dynamics in nonequilibrium processes.

This course is strongly encouraged for graduate students in chemistry and engineering whose research will involve dynamic chemical processes and the use of any spectroscopic method to understand them (e.g., photochemistry, lasers, catalysis, batteries, materials design and synthesis, atmospheric chemistry, chemical reaction engineering and reactor design, electrochemistry, nanoscience, and more!)

This course is structured to enhance graduate students' ability to understand aspects of their research more deeply and to benefit their progress in graduate school. The course also aims to provide opportunities to seed research collaborations through a brief final group-based project.

course_details.Overview of class: This course will focus on the fundamentals and applications of light and its interactions with materials. We will discuss the properties of different materials, relate microscopic descriptions to measured macroscopic properties, connect how size, shape, and structure affect optical properties, and be exposed to state-of-the-art tools necessary for research in nanophotonics. These concepts will be applied and integrated into modern research problems at Northwestern University and applications of current technical interest in society.

course_details.Topic: Spin Quantum Physics and Magnetic Resonance
course_details.Overview of class: This course will focus on concepts in Magnetic Resonance and Quantum Information Science, beginning with the foundations of the quantum mechanics of two-level systems and then applying these concepts across a wide range of topics in solution NMR, solid-state NMR, polarization transfer, and quantum information science. Topics will include introduction to quantum mechanics of two-level systems, the density matrix formalism, spin hamiltonians, time evolution, strong and weak coupling regimes, the product operator formalism, 2D pulse sequences, solid-state NMR, dynamic nuclear polarization, light-activated radical pair systems, nitrogen vacancy centers, and quantum gates and quantum algorithms from the perspective of spin magnetic resonance spectroscopy. This course will begin from the fundamentals before advancing to more complex topics to make it accessible and informative for both novice and experts in magnetic resonance spectroscopy. Lectures will also include demos on the implementation of simulation methods and visualization tools for magnetic resonance. Weekly homework assignments will apply and extend concepts introduced in lecture to physical systems. The final project will be a presentation on a topic of choice in magnetic resonance. This is a graduate level course and will be designed to benefit the student's research directly or indirectly.
